nodes.title: Whether a Texas default judgment will be set aside on a motion for new trial — a genuinely discretionary, multi-factor judicial determination

derived_from.cite: Craddock v. Sunshine Bus Lines, Inc., 133 S.W.2d 124, 126 (Tex. 1939)
derived_from.quoted_text: A default judgment should be set aside and a new trial ordered in any case in which the failure of the defendant to answer before judgment was not intentional, or the result of conscious indifference on his part, but was due to a mistake or an accident; provided the motion for a new trial sets up a meritorious defense and is filed at a time when the granting thereof will occasion no delay or otherwise work an injury to the plaintiff.

derived_from.quoted_text: A motion for new trial, if filed, shall be filed prior to or within thirty days after the judgment or other order complained of is signed.

derived_from.quoted_text: In the event an original or amended motion for new trial or a motion to modify, correct or reform a judgment is not determined by written order signed within seventy-five days after the judgment was signed, it shall be considered overruled by operation of law on expiration of that period.

derived_from.quoted_text: (b) Motion to Set Aside Default. A defendant against whom a default judgment is granted may file a motion to set aside the judgment no later than 14 days after the judgment is signed. The defendant must serve the plaintiff with a copy of the motion no later than the next business day using a method approved under Rule 501.4. The court may set aside the judgment and set the case for trial for good cause shown. ... (e) Motion Denied as a Matter of Law. If the judge has not ruled on a motion to set aside, motion to reinstate, or motion for new trial, the motion is automatically denied at 5:00 p.m. on the 21st day after the day the judgment was signed.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the JUSTICE COURT variant of the set-aside deadline the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- this node previously hard-coded the TRCP 329b(a)/(c) district/county court deadlines (30 days to file, 75 days to overrule-by-operation-of-law) as if they applied universally, but justice-court (small-claims-tier) default judgments -- among the most common in Texas consumer debt collection -- are governed by the much shorter TRCP 505.3 (14 days to file, denied by operation of law at day 21 if not ruled on). A justice-court defendant told she has 30 days would be told she is timely when her actual window has already closed. Source is a law school's rules-history repository (not an official state site) because the official Texas courts rules PDF was not independently re-fetched this session -- tagged C (secondary aggregator, corroborating only) rather than B, and flagged for live verification against txcourts.gov before relying on the exact deadline language. CORRECTED 2026-09-02 (round 37): the prior quoted_text was a paraphrase, not a quote -- '(a) Motion to Reinstate.' (actual heading: 'Motion to Reinstate after Dismissal.'), 'order of dismissal' (actual: 'dismissal order'), '(b) Motion to Set Aside Default Judgment' (actual: 'Motion to Set Aside Default'), and a '(d) Ruling' subsection that does not exist (the automatic-denial rule is (e)). Failed live at prefix 23 (run_20260902T185148Z.json). Re-verified verbatim against a fresh fetch of the cited stcl.edu page. The node's logic (14 days; automatic denial at 5:00 p.m. on the 21st day) was already correct.

derived_from.quoted_text: (4) ... if within twenty days after the judgment or other appealable order is signed, a party adversely affected by it or his attorney has neither received the notice required by paragraph (3) of this rule nor acquired actual knowledge of the order, then with respect to that party all the periods mentioned in paragraph (1) shall begin on the date that such party or his attorney received such notice or acquired actual knowledge of the signing, whichever occurred first, but in no event shall such periods begin more than ninety days after the original judgment or other appealable order was signed. (5) In order to establish the application of paragraph (4) ... the party adversely affected is required to prove in the trial court, on sworn motion and notice, the date on which the party or his attorney first either received a notice of the judgment or acquired actual knowledge of the signing.
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) to encode the notice-restart mechanism the corroboration pipeline's adversarial check found missing -- this node's checklist previously treated 'more than 30 days since signing' as an absolute, unconditional bar, but TRCP 306a(4)-(5) restarts the deadline from actual notice/knowledge (up to 90 days after signing) on a sworn motion, for a defendant who genuinely didn't learn of the judgment in time -- a common fact pattern when notice went to a stale address and the debtor first learns of the judgment via a garnishment or credit report hit. Same C-tier/verification caveat as the § 505.3 entry above.

derived_from.cite: Peralta v. Heights Medical Center, Inc., 485 U.S. 80 (1988); Tex. R. App. P. 30; bill of review (4-year limit)
derived_from.quoted_text: Peralta held that a default judgment entered without proper service violates due process regardless of whether the defendant had a meritorious defense -- a defendant who was never validly served is not required to show the Craddock meritorious-defense element to attack the judgment. In Texas, a defendant who missed the 30-day/505.3 window (and any 306a notice-restart) because of defective or absent service may still pursue a restricted appeal within 6 months of judgment (Tex. R. App. P. 26.1(c), 30 -- available to a party who did not participate at trial, where the error is apparent on the face of the record) or a bill of review within 4 years of judgment (an equitable proceeding to set aside a judgment no longer subject to appeal or new-trial motion).
derived_from.tier_rationale: Added 2026-08-30 (round 22) -- Peralta is a controlling U.S. Supreme Court due-process holding (confirmed via WebSearch of multiple case-law summaries and the restricted-appeal/bill-of-review deadline sources this session), but the surrounding Texas procedural mechanics (restricted appeal, bill of review) are commentary/secondary-source-confirmed rather than independently fetched from a primary Texas court rules site this session -- tagged D, corroboration only, flagged for live verification rather than treated as fully primary-sourced. This is squarely a BAND 3 addition: it does not predict any outcome, it only names an additional remedy path and its own deterministic filing deadlines, consistent with this node's existing 'what_the_system_may_say' discipline.

derived_from.quoted_text: (e) No Motion For New Trial. No motion for new trial may be filed.

derived_from.quoted_text: (a) How Taken; Time. A party may appeal a judgment in an eviction case by filing a bond, making a cash deposit, or filing a sworn statement of inability to pay with the justice court within 5 days after the judgment is signed.

logic.concept: BAND 3 -- GENUINELY DISCRETIONARY. This node's only honest output is the boundary marker itself: flagging that a default judgment may be set aside, naming the three factors a Texas court weighs, and stating who bears the burden -- never predicting whether a specific court will actually grant the motion. Predicting the outcome of a discretionary judicial determination is out of scope for this system by design (see spec Band taxonomy, docs/GLOSSARY.md) -- this is a permanent boundary, not a gap to close with more data.
logic.trigger: A default judgment (or a judgment following an answer with a subsequent failure to appear, per Ivy v. Carrell, 407 S.W.2d 212 (Tex. 1966), extending Craddock) has already been entered against the person, and the person wants to know whether it can be reopened.
craddock_factors_named_not_applied: (1) the failure to answer was not intentional or the result of conscious indifference, but the result of an accident or mistake
(2) the motion for new trial sets up a meritorious defense
(3) granting the motion will occasion no undue delay or otherwise injure the plaintiff
logic.procedural_deadline_component_this_IS_de: The motion for new trial must be filed within 30 days after the judgment is signed (TRCP 329b(a)) -- Band 1 within an otherwise Band 3 node. If it is not decided by written signed order within 75 days of judgment, it is overruled by operation of law (TRCP 329b(c)). Missing the 30-day window forecloses this path entirely regardless of how strong the three Craddock factors are -- this deterministic gate should be surfaced to the user with urgency distinct from the discretionary merits question.
logic.what_the_system_may_say: Name the three-factor test, explain each factor in plain language, flag the 30-day filing deadline as hard and case-critical, and tell the person a licensed attorney's judgment is needed to assess factors (1) and (2) against their specific facts. Also: identify which court entered the judgment (district/county vs. justice court) since the filing deadline differs; flag whether the TRCP 306a notice-restart may apply if the person says they only recently learned of the judgment; and flag whether service is disputed at all, since that changes which remedy (Craddock motion vs. restricted appeal vs. bill of review) is even the right one to pursue -- these are the same kind of deterministic, non-discretionary gates as the existing 30-day filing deadline, not predictions of a discretionary outcome.
logic.what_the_system_may_NOT_say: Any prediction of whether a specific court will grant or deny the motion; any characterization of the person's facts as clearly meeting or failing a factor; any percentage or likelihood language.
logic.justice_court_variant_note: The 30-day/75-day TRCP 329b deadlines above apply in DISTRICT OR COUNTY COURT. If the default judgment was entered in JUSTICE COURT (small-claims-tier, common for consumer debt-buyer suits), the governing deadline is instead TRCP 505.3: 14 days to file a motion to set aside/for new trial, denied by operation of law at 5:00 p.m. on the 21st day if not ruled on. Which court entered the judgment is a threshold, deterministic fact this node must ask before applying either deadline -- like the 30-day TRCP 329b deadline itself, this is Band 1 within an otherwise Band 3 node, not a matter of discretion.
logic.notice_restart_note: The filing deadline (30 days under 329b, or 14 days under 505.3) is NOT an absolute bar if the party did not receive notice of the judgment or acquire actual knowledge of it within 20 days after signing. TRCP 306a(4)-(5) restarts the deadline from the date of actual notice/knowledge (up to 90 days after the original signing), on a sworn motion proving that later notice date. A defendant who first learns of a default judgment via a bank garnishment, wage withholding, or credit-report hit weeks after signing may still have a live path -- this deterministic gate should be checked before concluding the window has closed.
logic.defective_service_note: If service was defective or never happened at all, the Craddock three-factor test (and the meritorious-defense showing it requires) does NOT govern -- Peralta v. Heights Medical Center holds a defendant who was never properly served need not show a meritorious defense at all, because entering judgment without valid service violates due process independent of the merits. Such a defendant, even outside the 329b/505.3/306a windows, may still have a restricted appeal (within 6 months of judgment) or a bill of review (within 4 years) available -- this node should not tell a defendant with a live service defect that no remedy remains just because the ordinary motion-for-new-trial windows have closed.

logic.eviction_carve_out_note: ADDED 2026-09-03 (round 38) -- CASE-ENDING if missed: the justice-court branch (TRCP 505.3, 14 days) does NOT apply to an EVICTION (forcible detainer) default. Eviction cases are governed by TRCP 510, which controls over the general justice-court rules; TRCP 510.8(e) bars a motion for new trial in an eviction case, and the operative remedy is an appeal (bond, cash deposit, or sworn statement of inability) within FIVE days of the judgment under TRCP 510.9, after which a writ of possession can issue. Directing an evicted tenant to a 14-day motion blows the 5-day deadline. Appeared in both backlog runs.
logic.restricted_appeal_not_limited_to_service: ADDED 2026-09-03 (round 38): this node offered the restricted appeal (Tex. R. App. P. 30, six months) and the bill of review only in the 'defective/no service' branch. That is too narrow. A restricted appeal requires only that the party did not participate in the hearing, filed within six months, and that error is apparent on the face of the record -- defective service is merely the most common such error; an unsupported unliquidated-damages award, a facially defective return of service, or a missing TRCP 239a certificate qualify equally. And a bill of review (four years) is available to a validly-served defendant who never received notice of the judgment through no fault of her own (e.g. the clerk never mailed the TRCP 306a notice and she learned of it only via garnishment months later), with a potentially lower showing than the ordinary Baker v. Goldsmith elements. As encoded, a consumer who concedes service but was hit with an inflated default months ago would be told no path remains. Case-law gloss, source_tier C, flagged for counsel confirmation.

completeness_checklist.fact: Has a default judgment (or dismissal-for-failure-to-appear judgment) actually been entered, and on what date was it signed?
Is the person still within 30 days of the judgment being signed? (Deterministic gate -- if no, this path is foreclosed regardless of the merits.)
Why did the person fail to answer or appear -- their own account of what happened (raw input for factor 1; the system does not characterize it)
Does the person have a defense to the underlying claim, and what is it (raw input for factor 2; the system does not characterize it)
Which court entered the default judgment -- district/county court (TRCP 329b: 30/75 days) or justice court (TRCP 505.3: 14/21 days)

When the person actually learned of the judgment (received notice or otherwise gained actual knowledge) -- if more than 20 days after signing, TRCP 306a(4)-(5) may restart the filing deadline from that later date, up to 90 days after signing, on a sworn motion

Whether the person disputes that they were validly served at all (defective/no service) -- if so, Craddock's meritorious-defense element does not apply, and a restricted appeal (6 months) or bill of review (4 years) may be available even after the ordinary motion window has closed

THRESHOLD: is the underlying case an EVICTION (forcible detainer)? If so, TRCP 510 governs -- no motion for new trial (510.8(e)); the remedy is an appeal within 5 days of judgment (510.9). Do not apply the 14-day 505.3 window

Even if service was valid: (a) is it within six months of the judgment and is there error apparent on the face of the record (e.g. unsupported damages) -- restricted appeal; (b) did the defendant never receive notice of the judgment through no fault of her own -- bill of review within four years

consequences_and_next_steps.action: If within 30 days of the judgment being signed, file (or get help filing) a motion for new trial immediately -- this deadline is hard and does not extend for weighing the merits first.
consequences_and_next_steps.deadline_detail: 30 days from the date the judgment was signed, per Tex. R. Civ. P. 329b(a)

consequences_and_next_steps.action: Consult a licensed Texas attorney to assess whether the three Craddock factors are met on the specific facts -- this is a discretionary judicial determination this system does not and will not predict.

If more than 30 days but less than 75 days have passed and no written order has issued, the motion (if filed in time) will be overruled by operation of law at the 75-day mark -- flag this to the person as a status check, not a new filing deadline.
consequences_and_next_steps.deadline_detail: 75 days from the date the judgment was signed, per Tex. R. Civ. P. 329b(c)
